problem: Existing VLN agents follow explicit instructions and cannot infer users' implicit intentions; they also do not reuse past experience in persistent environments across episodes (no memory of scene maps for renavigation).
motivation: Real-world users give implicit, high-level requests (e.g. stating a need rather than a target), and agents operating over time in the same environment should exploit accumulated scene knowledge. This calls for persistent scene memory plus LLM reasoning over instructions, observations and maps.
key_idea: Build and store explicit scene maps across episodes and let an LLM jointly reason over the instruction, observations and map to emit semantic navigation tokens that guide action prediction, trained hierarchically (navigation first, then scene associations for implicit-instruction reasoning).
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablation evidence can be cited. The abstract implies that persistent explicit maps and a two-stage curriculum (actions first, then scene-association reasoning) are what enable implicit-instruction reasoning and improved renavigation.
method: Explicit scene map construction: builds and stores maps of the environment persistently so later episodes can reuse them for renavigation and learn scene associations.
LLM-based reasoning: an LLM jointly processes user instruction, agent observations and scene maps to comprehend implicit instructions.
Semantic navigation tokens: the LLM generates tokens that guide action prediction.
Hierarchical learning paradigm: stage 1 learns navigation actions; stage 2 learns scene associations for implicit instruction reasoning.
Implicit instruction benchmark: a new dataset for training and evaluating reasoning-based iterative navigation.
